metadata.title: Soft Edges, Glow and Noise
metadata.topic: GODOT SHADERS · SOFT EDGES, GLOW AND NOISE
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How to soften edges, layer effects, and add glow
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Soft Edges, Glow and Noise. Learn how to soften an edge, layer a highlight on top, scroll noise through it, and make glow work for real, so your effects stop looking flat.

routing.reason: The lecture skill's approved first beat: portrait, title, narrated summary.

shot.visual_intent: Professor Bear portrait, exact film title and short payoff visible immediately.

show.event: Complete populated lecture opener visible for the whole narration

qc.sparse_reason: Identity card: portrait and title; teaching motion resumes in BIDEA.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people think a soft edge needs a blur. It does not. A soft edge is a ramp: a value that climbs from zero to one over a distance you choose. We will build one bubble a layer at a time, and finish with glow.

props.text: A soft edge needs a blur.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A ramp is a smooth run of values from zero to one. A mask is a number from zero to one for each pixel: how much to show. U V is a pixel's address on the shape. A uniform is a value your game sets. Alpha is how visible a pixel is.

terms.meaning: a smooth run of values from 0 up to 1
a number from 0 to 1 per pixel saying how much of something to show
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one
how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: prerequisites, one plain line each.

beats.narration_text: One circle, drawn two ways. First, an edge sharp enough to cut a finger. Then the same circle with the edge fading softly into the background. Nothing was blurred. One function made the difference.

Labels 'hard edge' then 'soft edge'.

beats.narration_text: The hard edge comes from a function called step. Give it a line in the sand, and a value. Below the line, it answers zero. At the line or above, one. Nothing in between.

shot.visual_intent: Axes on the cream stage: horizontal x from 0 to 1, vertical result 0 to 1. A grey dashed vertical line at the edge 0.4, labelled 'edge'. A terracotta dot slides along the bottom at height 0 from the left; when it crosses the line it jumps up to height 1 and runs on along the top, leaving a cliff-shaped curve behind it. Beneath the axes the GLOSSARY wording: 'step(edge, x): 0 below the edge, 1 from the edge up'.

show.event: dot jumps to one; cliff curve drawn

shot.motion_claim: The dot slides along zero, jumps to one at the line, and the curve behind it is a cliff.

beats.narration_text: A circle is a distance test. Distance asks how far apart two points are. Ask it how far each pixel's address is from the middle. One minus a step on that answer is one inside the radius, and zero outside.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the hard-disc shader); at right a real Godot window with the teal disc and its razor-sharp edge. A terracotta ring settles on the right-hand part of the rim. A label on each highlighted line defines distance and step (GLOSSARY wording).

show.event: step line + definition label; ring on the rim

cues.label: distance(a, b): how far apart two points are
step(edge, x): 0 below the edge, 1 from the edge up

beats.narration_text: Zoom in on that edge. Every pixel is either all color or none. With nothing in between, the rim becomes a staircase of square steps. That is why hard edges look jagged.

A terracotta outline walks along the boundary one step at a time. Caption: 'no in-between values'.

beats.narration_text: Smooth step takes two lines. Below the first, zero. Above the second, one. Between them, it climbs along a smooth curve: slow to start, fastest in the middle, slow to finish.

shot.visual_intent: Axes: horizontal x from 0 to 0.5, vertical result 0 to 1. Two grey dashed vertical lines at a = 0.25 and b = 0.4, labelled 'a' and 'b'. A terracotta dot rides along the x axis; the curve behind it is flat at 0, S-shaped between the two lines, then flat at 1. Rule label under the plot in two lines, in the GLOSSARY wording (the two edges are the dashed lines a and b): 'smoothstep(a, b, x): a switch that eases in and out between two edges:' then '0 below a, 1 above b, a smooth S between'.

show.event: axes with lines a and b
S-shaped climb between a and b

shot.motion_claim: The dot rides along and the curve it leaves is flat, then an S, then flat again.

lecture.why: A curve that bends between two lines is a plot; the dot makes 'slow, fast, slow' visible as speed.

beats.narration_text: That curve is not a straight line. Ten percent of the way along, a straight ramp reads zero point one. Smooth step reads zero point zero two eight. The formula is three t squared minus two t cubed.

shot.visual_intent: The same plot in unit form: t (labelled 'how far along the band, 0 to 1') from 0 to 1, a grey dashed diagonal (the straight ramp) and the terracotta S-curve. At t = 0.1 a vertical marker with two dots: the straight ramp at 0.1 and the curve at 0.028, a bracket between them. At t = 0.5 the dots coincide at 0.5. Typeset at top right: 3t^2 - 2t^3 (real MathTex, per docs/MATH-TYPESETTING.md) and under it, in monospace and labelled as code, t * t * (3.0 - 2.0 * t).

show.event: marker at t = 0.1, dots 0.1 and 0.028, bracket
marker moves to t = 0.5: dots coincide

shot.motion_claim: The marker lands at ten percent and the two dots split: 0.1 on the line, 0.028 on the curve.

beats.narration_text: Swap step for smooth step and give it two radii. Inside zero point two five, fully on. Beyond zero point four, fully off. In between, the value glides down. That band is the soft edge.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the soft-disc shader, one line changed from the hard disc); at right the real render: the teal disc whose edge fades over a band. A terracotta ring on the band at the right side, small labels '0.25' and '0.4' at the band's two ends.

beats.narration_text: Tie the inner radius to a uniform and you get a softness dial. Small values give a crisp rim. Large ones give a cloud. The outer radius never moves.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the soft-width shader); at right a real Godot window whose disc starts with a crisp rim and, as softness is swept up, spreads into a cloud while the outer edge stays put. Labels 'crisp' then 'cloud'.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · softness swept by script

lecture.capture_spec: C04: the square target, lab-shaders/03-soft-width.gdshader, softness 0.02 held 1 s, swept to 0.4 by 7 s, held (`--animate softness:0:0.02,1:0.02,7:0.4`); 12 s, 30 fps, Forward+. Verified stills: softness 0.05 gives 6,448 in-between pixels, 0.15 gives 16,780, 0.4 gives 27,400; outer edge unchanged.

beats.narration_text: Squeeze the band to nothing, and smooth step becomes step. But the docs call equal lines undefined, and the range on that uniform cannot stop code from sending zero. So keep the width above zero with max.

shot.visual_intent: The S-curve plot with its two lines a and b. The lines slide together; the S-curve steepens into a vertical cliff, a step, at the moment they touch. At the touch a label 'a = b: undefined (docs)' and, in grey, 'this Mac: a hard cut' with the small grey credit 'Apple M4 Pro · Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ and Compatibility'. Then a code chip slides in beside it: max(softness, 0.01), with the label 'max(a, b): the larger of two values'.

shot.motion_claim: The two dashed lines slide together and the smooth curve collapses into a cliff.

beats.narration_text: You will also meet smooth step with its lines swapped, to flip the ramp. On this Mac that worked. The docs still call it undefined, so write one minus smooth step instead.

beats.narration_text: A falloff is how quickly a value fades as you move away from a point. The simplest is one minus the distance: one at the point, dropping steadily to zero a whole unit away.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Falloff and Highlight' (serif 40) top-left. An 11-by-11 pixel grid of outline cells with a terracotta spot on the cell left of centre. Concentric distance rings expand from the spot; each cell fills teal in proportion to 1 minus its distance, with its number written on one row: 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, 0.0. At right a profile: value against distance, a straight line falling from 1 to 0 at distance 1. Label 'falloff: how quickly a value fades with distance'.

shot.motion_claim: The rings spread from the spot and the cells behind them fill less and less, down to zero at distance one.

beats.narration_text: Make the power a uniform and watch the spot shrink as it climbs. Power one is a haze, three a soft highlight, eight a pinpoint. The clamp stops the number going negative, where a power is undefined.

beats.narration_text: A falloff never stops by itself, so cut it to a shape. Multiply it by the circle's mask, the disc. Where the disc is zero, the product is zero, and the highlight can only show on the bubble.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the spot-in-disc shader); at right a real Godot window: first the teal spot with its faint tail running past where the bubble will be, then at the swap the tail beyond the disc vanishes and the highlight is confined to the disc. A terracotta ring on the tail beyond the disc with readouts '0.09' then '0'.

beats.narration_text: A layer is a color plus a mask: how much of that color to show. The body is teal, masked by the disc. The highlight is pale, masked by the spot. Stack them and you have a bubble.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Layering' (serif 40) top-left. Two sheets slide in over the stage: a teal disc sheet labelled 'body · mask: the disc' and a pale highlight sheet labelled 'highlight · mask: the spot'. They slide together into one bubble (a teal disc with a pale highlight) that settles where they met.

lecture.why: Two things becoming one is the idea of layering; a flat slide-together keeps the cast (disc, spot) the viewer already knows.

beats.narration_text: Two ways to combine masks. Multiply, and you keep only where both are on. Add, and you get where either is on, up to a cap of one. Multiply by zero erases. Add zero and nothing changes.

shot.visual_intent: Two overlapping discs A (teal outline) and B (pale outline) with four sample points: in both, only A, only B, in neither. A left column 'multiply' lights the lens where both are one and writes each point's product: 1, 0, 0, 0. A right column 'add' lights the union and writes the sums: 2 (capped to 1), 1, 1, 0.

beats.narration_text: Now the sum. The body color, plus the highlight color times the highlight mask. Where the mask is zero, nothing is added. Where it is one, the highlight color lands in full.

beats.narration_text: A trap. Add a brightness dial for the whole bubble. Multiplication always happens before addition. So a plus b times c multiplies b and c first, and only the highlight dims. Wrap the sum in parentheses.

shot.visual_intent: The expression a + b * c as a small tree: b * c is ringed first (terracotta), then the plus. Beneath it the parenthesised (a + b) * c with the plus ringed first. Numbers on the leaves: a = 0.64 (the body, green channel), b = 0.52 (the highlight, green channel), c = 0.6 (brightness); results written under each: 0.95 and 0.70. Label 'multiply binds first'.

show.event: right tree (a + b) * c; ring on a + b; result 0.70

shot.motion_claim: The ring lands on b * c first in the left tree and on a + b first in the right one, and the two results differ.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A soft edge is a ramp, and smooth step lets you choose its width. A falloff fades with distance, and a power tightens it. Multiply masks to keep both, add them to show either. Wrap a sum in parentheses before you scale it. Noise gives structure, time scrolls it, repeat and seamless keep it going. A color above one glows only when the shader, the viewport and the environment agree.
